c.tagline: Sardinia's sun-baked capital: hilltop Castello, Roman ruins, and Poetto beach.

taxi.fareNote: Uber does not operate in Cagliari or Sardinia; use the official white metered taxis at ranks, or phone/app-book a radio taxi (Radiotaxi 4 Mori and Rossoblu). Fares are metered with supplements for luggage and night rides.

emergency.note: 112 is the single EU emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Castello: Castello district Cagliari Bastione Saint Remy

avoid.reason: Minor bag and beach-belonging theft around the Marina district, the station and Poetto beach in summer.

hood_desc: Cagliari's oldest quarter, a walled citadel on the hill wrapped in medieval towers, the cathedral and the Bastione di Saint Remy terraces; steep, atmospheric streets with the best views, ideal for sightseeing (mind the stairs and few elevators).

The flat, lively grid between the Castello hill and the port, packed with restaurants, wine bars and shops along Via Roma; the easiest first-time base with great transport links, though it can be noisy at night.
The prettiest of the old quarters, a residential neighborhood of pastel houses, artisan workshops and the Basilica of San Saturnino; quieter and lived-in, a short walk east of the center.
The most authentic working old quarter, home to the Roman amphitheatre, the botanical gardens and everyday markets; central and walkable but calm at night, a good local base.

Cagliari's famous beach district, a long white-sand strip backed by lidos, kiosks and cycle paths along the Marina Piccola and the Molentargius salt flats with their flamingos; a relaxed, sun-and-sea base a bus ride from the center.

water.note: Tap water is safe, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: CTM buses run roughly 5:30am to around midnight, with a limited late-night 'Linea Notte' on weekends; the Metrocagliari light rail runs daytime into mid-evening.
transit.note: Getting around blends CTM's dense city bus network with the two-line Metrocagliari light rail (ARST) that runs north from Piazza Repubblica to the suburbs; the historic center is best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Buy CTM tickets (about €1.30 for 90 minutes) at tobacconists, machines or the CTM/DropTicket app before boarding, and validate on board; you can also tap a contactless bank card on many buses. The Metrocagliari light rail uses the same integrated tickets.

ferry: Port of Cagliari (Via Roma cruise & ferry terminal)

transit.m: Trenitalia train to Cagliari Centrale (~7 min)
CTM/ARST bus to city center (~15 min)

tip.r: A service or cover charge (coperto) is often on the bill; rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is enough.

landmarks: Bastione di Saint Remy
A grandiose limestone terrace crowning the Castello quarter, its sweeping staircases and umbrella pines frame Cagliari's rooftops, lagoons, and the shimmering Gulf of Angels.
Castello (Old Citadel Quarter)
Cagliari's walled hilltop heart tangles medieval alleys between Pisan towers and aristocratic palazzi, delivering sea views from nearly every sun-bleached rampart.
Cattedrale di Santa Maria (Cagliari Cathedral)
A 13th-century Pisan church remodeled in exuberant baroque, treasuring intricately carved Romanesque pulpits and a glittering crypt hewn with hundreds of rosettes.
Torre dell'Elefante
This 1307 Pisan defense tower, named for the small marble elephant on its facade, still bears its medieval portcullis and offers vertiginous city views.
Spiaggia del Poetto
Eight kilometers of soft white sand minutes from downtown, where locals swim, sip spritzes at kiosks, and stroll beneath the saddle-shaped Sella del Diavolo headland.
Museo Archeologico Nazionale
Sardinia's premier museum guards the enigmatic bronze figurines and towering Mont'e Prama giants of the mysterious Nuragic civilization, unique in the Mediterranean world.
Anfiteatro Romano (Roman Amphitheatre)
Carved directly into a rocky hillside in the 2nd century AD, this amphitheatre once hosted gladiatorial spectacles for up to 10,000 Roman spectators.
Parco di Molentargius-Saline
Thousands of pink flamingos wade and nest in these former salt pans, an extraordinary urban wetland reachable by bicycle from the Poetto beachfront.
Santuario di Nostra Signora di Bonaria
Sailors' basilica and Sardinia's most important pilgrimage site, home to a miraculous 14th-century Madonna that washed ashore in a crate from a shipwreck.
Mercato di San Benedetto
One of Italy's largest covered markets, a two-story feast of glistening tuna, bottarga, pecorino, and banter that reveals Cagliari's soul before noon.

train.note: No international trains - Sardinia is an island with no rail link to the mainland. Trenitalia runs the island network from Cagliari north to Oristano, Macomer and Sassari/Olbia, taking around four hours to Olbia; the separate narrow-gauge ARST 'Trenino Verde' operates scenic tourist routes in summer. Regional fares are fixed-price.

bus.note: No international coaches. ARST (https://www.arst.sardegna.it/) runs the island bus network from the Piazza Matteotti terminal beside the station, reaching Villasimius, Pula and the Costa Rei beaches; Turmo Travel runs the fast link north to Olbia and Santa Teresa. Buses are often better than trains for the coast.

intl.to: Civitavecchia (Rome), Naples & Palermo (Italy) - ~13 hr to Civitavecchia

ferry.note: Cagliari's ferry terminal is right at the foot of the old town, a few minutes' walk from the centre. The overnight crossings to Civitavecchia are the main link to Rome and carry cars; sailings are more frequent in summer and can be cancelled in winter storms. There is no direct international route - for Corsica or mainland Europe you sail via Porto Torres or Olbia in the north of the island.
